strengths: Soundness: Theorem 3.1 provides a useful equivalence between local and global updates under explicit linearity, orthonormality, and optimal-head assumptions. Theorem 3.3 adds a narrower result for direct feedback, and the simulations systematically examine departures from these assumptions.

Significance: Spatially dependent projections substantially improve local learning. Table 2 reports gains over the spatially independent variant from 73.21% to 80.51% on CIFAR-10, 75.10% to 78.66% on STL-10, and 28.18% to 36.63% on Tiny-ImageNet. These are meaningful improvements within the evaluated setting.

Originality: The main contribution is the connection between local contrastive learning and global gradients, together with its use to motivate spatially structured projections and learned direct feedback. This provides useful understanding beyond another local-loss variant.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript has a coherent theory-to-experiment progression, informative ablations, and architectural and optimization details in Appendix B. Principal accuracy results include confidence intervals across four seeds.

Limitations and ethics: The authors explicitly acknowledge that the equivalence does not extend to nonlinear networks or normalized Forward-Forward algorithms, and that their BP baseline is not state of the art. These are appropriate qualifications. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for the benchmark-based study.
weaknesses: Soundness: Definition 3.4 does not establish the claimed theoretical upper bound on cosine similarity. Minimizing dataset-averaged squared error between activation gradients need not maximize cosine similarity between weight gradients. Numerical optimization is also not shown to attain a global optimum, and the comparison trains different encoders rather than evaluating competing projections at identical encoder weights. Consequently, Figures 3B and 4C support comparison with a gradient-matching heuristic, not the claim that local learning is almost the ideal BP approximation.

Evidence for matching BP is mixed. On STL-10, the best local method reaches 79.62 ± 0.28%, versus 80.36 ± 0.26% for BP-CLAPP++ and 81.97 ± 1.23% for BP-InfoNCE; the reported intervals do not overlap. CIFAR-10 and Tiny-ImageNet support competitive performance, but the across-dataset matching claim needs qualification or a defined equivalence criterion. The statement that all spatial variants outperform SCFF on all datasets is also inconsistent with CIFAR-10 results of 80.51% for CLAPP++ and 80.60% for SCFF.

The comparisons do not fully isolate the source of the advantage. Published local-method results are combined with new experiments without establishing matched augmentation, readout, and training protocols. The proposed method concatenates representations from multiple layers, but the baseline descriptions do not explicitly establish identical readout features across comparisons. Spatial dependence also expands the projection parameterization, without parameter counts or a capacity-matched control separating spatial structure from additional capacity.

Reproducibility remains incomplete for important implementation choices. The manuscript does not provide a code link, exact augmentation parameters, InfoNCE temperature, linear-probe training duration, or a fully explicit specification of spatial projection tensor shapes and loss aggregation. Appendix C additionally reports selecting the best supervised accuracy over test-set evaluations, which biases that auxiliary comparison and should be replaced by validation-based selection.

Presentation and theoretical scope need tightening. The Forward-Forward description reverses the conventional positive/negative goodness direction, and Table 1 substitutes a linear loss without clearly distinguishing this simplification from the original algorithm. Theorem 3.1 also relies on references transforming consistently across layers, a condition not explicitly included in its statement and not generally satisfied by the independently chosen fixed references listed for PhyLL. These issues weaken the claimed breadth of the unified formalism.

strengths: Originality: The connection between local contrastive learning and global SSL gradients provides useful theoretical understanding. Theorem 3.1 establishes an interpretable equivalence under explicit orthogonality and optimal-head assumptions, while Theorem 3.3 motivates direct feedback in a restricted dimensionality-reduction setting.

Significance: Spatially dependent projections produce substantial empirical improvements. In Table 2, adding spatial dependence increases accuracy from 73.21 to 80.51 on CIFAR-10, 75.10 to 78.66 on STL-10, and 28.18 to 36.63 on Tiny-ImageNet. These are meaningful gains for local representation learning.

Soundness: The paper includes assumption-removal experiments, spatial-dependence and feedback ablations, three image benchmarks, and four-seed confidence intervals for its principal results. Comparisons against backpropagation using the same backbone and related objectives are useful controlled experiments.

Presentation, reproducibility, and ethics: The progression from linear-network analysis to practical modifications is generally clear. Appendix B supplies architecture, optimizer, training duration, and spatial pooling settings. The authors explicitly acknowledge that their theory does not extend to nonlinear networks and that their BP baseline is not state of the art. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: Definition 3.4 does not establish the claimed theoretical upper bound on cosine similarity. Minimizing mean squared activation-gradient error need not maximize weight-gradient cosine similarity, and numerical training does not certify a global optimum. Moreover, separately training the purported optimal model changes the representations and BP gradients being compared. Consequently, the claim that local learning nearly attains the optimal BP approximation is unsupported. This should be presented as an empirical reference, or replaced with a justified bound evaluated at common frozen network states.

Scope of the theoretical evidence: Theorem 3.1 concerns instantaneous updates in orthogonal linear networks with fully optimized regularized projection matrices; the paper does not establish preservation of these conditions during training. Theorem 3.3 additionally requires a linear loss and batch size one. These are useful restricted results, but they do not establish that improved gradient alignment explains the nonlinear models' performance. Spatially dependent projections also increase flexibility, and no capacity-matched control separates that effect from improved BP approximation.

Empirical claims: Matching BP is dataset-dependent. On STL-10, the best local result is 79.62 ± 0.28, versus 80.36 ± 0.26 for BP-CLAPP++ and 81.97 ± 1.23 for BP-InfoNCE. The evidence supports approaching these particular baselines, rather than consistently matching them. Likewise, the statement that all spatial variants outperform SCFF on every dataset contradicts the CIFAR-10 results: CLAPP++ scores 80.51 versus SCFF's 80.60.

Comparability and reproducibility: The state-of-the-art comparison mixes results from prior publications with new experiments without establishing equivalent architectures, augmentation, and readout protocols. Multilayer concatenation is an important modification, but its application across comparison methods needs clearer documentation. The manuscript supplies no implementation link for the proposed method, and omits consequential details such as linear-probe training duration and complete augmentation settings.

Evaluation and presentation: Appendix C reports selecting the best supervised checkpoint using test accuracy, weakening that control experiment. Its broader negative conclusions about predictive coding also exceed what the limited implementation and tuning study establishes. Separately, Section 2 reverses the usual positive/negative goodness direction of Forward-Forward, conflicting with the increasing-positive-score formulation used later.

strengths: Soundness: Theorem 3.1 provides a useful equivalence between local and global SSL updates under explicit linearity, orthonormality, and optimal projection assumptions. The change-of-coordinates argument is convincing, and the numerical experiments systematically remove assumptions to examine their importance.

Originality: The contribution combines theoretical understanding with practical modifications: direct feedback from the final layer and spatially dependent predictive projections. The common formulation of several contrastive local learning rules helps explain their relationships.

Significance: Spatial dependence produces substantial improvements over the authors’ modified CLAPP baseline: 73.21% to 80.51% on CIFAR-10, 75.10% to 78.66% on STL-10, and 28.18% to 36.63% on Tiny ImageNet. These are useful advances for local representation learning.

Evaluation: Table 2 includes comparable backpropagation baselines, three datasets, and confidence intervals over four seeds for the principal methods. Ablations distinguish spatial dependence from direct feedback, and gradient measurements provide evidence beyond downstream accuracy.

Presentation and limitations: The progression from linear theory to nonlinear experiments is clear. The authors explicitly acknowledge that the equivalence does not extend to nonlinear networks or normalized Forward-Forward algorithms, and that their BP baseline is not state of the art. The work uses standard image benchmarks and presents no apparent material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: Definition 3.4 does not establish the claimed theoretical upper bound on weight-gradient cosine similarity. Minimizing activation-gradient squared error is a different objective, and multiplication by input activations changes the geometry of parameter gradients. Moreover, Appendix B trains separate encoders with different update rules, so their measurements do not establish optimality at a common network state. The comparator remains informative empirically, but the repeated near-optimality claims require correction or additional justification.

Empirical claims need qualification. On STL-10, the strongest local method achieves 79.62 ± 0.28%, versus 80.36 ± 0.26% for BP-CLAPP++ and 81.97 ± 1.23% for BP-InfoNCE. Thus, the results support approaching comparable BP performance, with matching results on some datasets, rather than uniformly closing the gap. The statement that all CLAPP++ variants outperform SCFF on every dataset is also contradicted by CIFAR-10: 80.51% versus 80.60%.

Reproducibility: Appendix B provides architecture, pooling sizes, optimizers, and training budgets, but omits several consequential details, including augmentation probabilities and strengths, linear-probe training duration, InfoNCE temperature, and precise reference-branch gradient handling. It also does not clearly establish whether all BP baselines use the same concatenated multilayer readout. No implementation link is provided.

Significance and comparison scope: Published local-learning results are compared without fully reconciling architecture, augmentation, and readout protocols. Spatially dependent projections also increase trainable capacity, but parameter counts and memory or runtime comparisons are absent. Consequently, the evidence supports a useful improvement within this experimental setting more strongly than an unqualified state-of-the-art or efficiency claim.

The theoretical guarantees concern highly restricted instantaneous updates; they do not establish that training preserves orthonormality or that finite-rate projection learning tracks its optimum. The nonlinear experiments are therefore essential empirical evidence, rather than validation of a general equivalence guarantee.

strengths: Originality: The orthogonal-change-of-coordinates argument in Theorem 3.1 provides useful understanding of when local and global SSL updates coincide. The shrinking-width analysis and spatial-feedback construction extend this perspective beyond the basic equivalence result.

Significance: Spatially structured projections substantially improve local learning across four datasets. For example, Table 2 shows improvements from 73.21% to 80.51% on CIFAR-10 and from 38.31% to 42.55% on ImageNet when spatial dependence is introduced.

Soundness: The experiments include matched-backbone BP baselines, component ablations, gradient-alignment measurements, and four-seed confidence intervals for the main smaller-dataset comparisons. These support the narrower conclusion that the proposed modifications improve local SSL.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript clearly connects theoretical analysis to algorithmic modifications and acknowledges the linear-network assumptions, restricted architectures, non-state-of-the-art BP baselines, and estimated nature of activation-memory savings. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: Definition 3.4 does not establish the claimed theoretical upper bound on weight-gradient cosine similarity. It minimizes dataset-averaged squared error between activation gradients, which is a different objective from cosine similarity between parameter gradients. Furthermore, the comparison trains separate networks, and numerical optimization does not certify a global optimum. Consequently, Figures 3B and 4C do not substantiate the repeated claim that the method is nearly the optimal local approximation to BP.

Soundness and reproducibility: The treatment of reference-branch gradients is inconsistent. Section 3.2 treats c as constant, and the theoretical updates omit differentiation through it. However, Algorithm 3 stops gradients only at layer inputs and computes losses using undetached c^l or c^L. As written, local losses differentiate through the reference branch; with DFB, losses from intermediate layers additionally update the final-layer weights. This prevents verification that the implemented algorithm matches the analyzed rule. Explicit reference detachment and complete update equations are needed.

Empirical claims: Table 2 does not support the assertion that the BP performance margin disappears on STL-10. The best local result is 79.62 ± 0.28%, versus 80.36 ± 0.26% for BP-CLAPP++ and 81.97 ± 1.23% for BP-InfoNCE. On ImageNet, the best local result is 44.16%, versus 48.52% and 55.19%. Matching is supported more convincingly on CIFAR-10 and Tiny-ImageNet; the abstract and conclusions should reflect this distinction.

Originality and comparison: Spatial dependence accounts for most of the empirical improvement, but related spatial implementations are acknowledged in Siddiqui et al. (2024), and SCFF already uses spatial dependence. Comparisons with published local-learning results do not establish matched architectures, augmentation, readout, or training budgets. The new theoretical interpretation is valuable, but a controlled comparison is needed to substantiate the broad local-SSL state-of-the-art claim.

Efficiency evidence: Table 3 estimates activation storage rather than measuring total training-memory requirements. The spatial matrices introduce potentially substantial parameter, gradient, and optimizer-state storage, which the estimate excludes. The manuscript honestly identifies this limitation, but the table cannot establish practical VRAM savings for CLAPP++ without end-to-end measurements including those costs.

Reproducibility: Appendix C supplies useful architectures and optimizer settings, but the manuscript's 'Code is available at' statement has no link. Projection initialization and optimization details, linear-probe training duration and selection protocol, and ImageNet variability are insufficiently documented. Together with the reference-gradient ambiguity, these omissions materially hinder independent reproduction.

strengths: Originality: The paper provides a useful theoretical connection between local contrastive learning and global SSL gradients. Theorem 3.1 identifies an interpretable equivalence under orthonormal linear transformations and optimized regularized projection matrices, while Theorem 3.3 motivates direct feedback under dimensionality reduction.

Significance: Spatially dependent projections substantially improve the local baseline across four datasets. In Table 2, CLAPP++ improves over its version without spatial dependence from 73.21% to 80.51% on CIFAR-10 and from 38.31% to 42.55% on ImageNet. These are meaningful improvements within local representation learning.

Evaluation: The paper combines mathematical analysis, controlled gradient-alignment experiments, downstream classification, and component ablations. Architecture-matched BP baselines are informative, and four-seed confidence intervals strengthen the results on the three smaller datasets.

Presentation and limitations: The main narrative is coherent, and the appendices provide substantial architectural and optimization details. The authors explicitly acknowledge that the exact theorem does not extend to nonlinear networks, that their BP baseline is not mainstream SSL state of the art, and that the memory-efficient algorithms were not used for full training. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: Definition 3.4 does not establish the claimed theoretical upper bound on gradient cosine similarity. It minimizes dataset-averaged squared error between activation gradients, whereas the figures measure cosine similarity between weight updates. These objectives are not generally equivalent. Moreover, the purported optimum is obtained by gradient descent while training a separate network, without a global-optimality guarantee or a comparison at identical encoder weights. Figures 3B and 4C therefore provide an empirical gradient-matching reference, not evidence that the proposed rule is nearly the best possible local approximation. This affects a central theoretical interpretation.

Soundness and reproducibility: The treatment of reference-branch gradients is inconsistent between the analysis and the implementation pseudocode. Section 3.2 treats c as constant with respect to W, but Algorithm 3 computes c^l = Layer_l(SG(c^{l-1})) and then uses c^l or c^L in the loss without detaching that output. As written, this permits additional reference-branch gradients; with direct feedback, intermediate losses also update the final-layer reference encoder. The manuscript needs an explicit stop-gradient convention and confirmation of which rule produced the results, since this determines whether the experiments implement the analyzed updates.

Claims versus evidence: Table 2 does not support the statement that the performance margin has disappeared on STL-10. The best local variant achieves 79.62 ± 0.28%, versus 80.36 ± 0.26% for BP-CLAPP++ and 81.97 ± 1.23% for BP-InfoNCE. On ImageNet, the best local result is 44.16%, versus 48.52% and 55.19%, respectively. Matching selected VGG baselines on CIFAR-10 and Tiny-ImageNet is useful, but the broader matching claims should be narrowed.

Mechanistic evidence and originality: Spatial dependence is the dominant empirical improvement, but it also greatly enlarges the trainable projection matrices. The paper acknowledges a related construction in Siddiqui et al. (2024), yet does not separate the benefits of spatial structure, additional projection capacity, and improved gradient alignment through capacity-controlled comparisons. The linear-network results motivate the design but do not establish that closer BP alignment explains its nonlinear-network performance.

Efficiency: Table 3 estimates activation storage rather than measuring total peak training memory. It omits the additional projection parameters, their gradients, and optimizer states, which are particularly relevant for the large spatially dependent matrices. The candid disclosure of this limitation is welcome, but the reported 38–60% activation-memory reduction cannot establish a corresponding practical VRAM advantage without full-training measurements.

Reproducibility and evaluation protocol: Appendix C omits important linear-probe details such as training duration and model-selection procedure, and ImageNet results lack uncertainty estimates. Appendix D explicitly selects the best supervised predictive-coding result using test accuracy across epochs; validation-based selection is needed for an unbiased comparison. These issues, together with the update-rule ambiguity and unsupported upper-bound interpretation, require revision before the contribution can be reliably built upon.

strengths: Soundness: The core linear-network analysis gives a useful, explicitly conditional connection between local and global SSL updates. Theorem 3.1 uses orthonormal weights and optimized, regularized projection matrices; Theorem 3.3 establishes a narrower direct-feedback result. Numerical experiments examine what happens when these assumptions are relaxed.

Significance: Spatially dependent local objectives produce substantial improvements across four datasets. In Table 2, adding spatial dependence increases CLAPP++ accuracy from 73.21% to 80.51% on CIFAR-10, 28.18% to 36.63% on Tiny-ImageNet, and 38.31% to 42.55% on ImageNet. These are useful advances for layerwise self-supervised learning.

Originality: The strongest contribution is the connection between gradient alignment, spatially structured projections, and representation quality. Although the individual ingredients have precedents, their theoretical interpretation and systematic combination provide new understanding.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript has a coherent progression from theory to algorithm design and evaluation. Appendix C supplies architectures, pooling configurations, optimizers, and training budgets; the smaller benchmark comparisons include four-seed confidence intervals. The authors appropriately acknowledge the restricted architectures, non-state-of-the-art BP baselines, and estimated nature of the memory savings. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: Definition 3.4 does not establish the claimed theoretical upper bound on cosine similarity. Minimizing squared error between activation gradients is not equivalent to maximizing cosine similarity between weight gradients, which also depend on presynaptic activities. Moreover, the numerical procedure trains different encoders and does not certify a global optimum. Figures 3B and 4C therefore support comparison with a gradient-matching reference, not the stronger claim that local learning is nearly optimal.

Significance and claim calibration: The statement that the performance margin has disappeared on all three smaller datasets is too strong. On STL-10, the best local result is 79.62 ± 0.28%, versus 80.36 ± 0.26% for BP-CLAPP++ and 81.97 ± 1.23% for BP-InfoNCE. On ImageNet, the best local result is 44.16%, versus 48.52% and 55.19%. The evidence supports substantial gap reduction and parity on selected benchmarks within the tested VGG setup.

Experimental attribution: Spatial dependence substantially enlarges the projection matrices, but there is no parameter-matched control separating spatial structure from increased auxiliary capacity. Likewise, improved alignment and accuracy occur together without establishing that alignment explains the accuracy gains. Comparisons with published local-learning methods also mix training and evaluation protocols, weakening the broad state-of-the-art claim.

Efficiency: Table 3 estimates activation storage rather than measuring total training memory, excluding potentially substantial spatial projection parameters, gradients, optimizer states, and temporary buffers. Full training uses Algorithm 3 rather than the proposed memory-saving implementations. Thus the reported savings do not yet establish a practical total-VRAM advantage.

Reproducibility: The reference-branch differentiation convention needs clarification. Section 3.2 treats c as constant, but Algorithm 3 does not explicitly detach c when constructing each loss. With direct feedback, this could allow lower-layer losses to update the final reference layer, changing the intended learning rule. The manuscript also leaves the code-availability statement without a usable link, and ImageNet results lack uncertainty estimates.
